extracted.intended_audience: university mathematics instructors and mathematicians interested in pedagogy and the future of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and standards for university-level mathematics teaching (objectives, problem selection, proof pedagogy, and fostering intellectual engagement) together with Weil's evaluative views on the nature and future of mathematical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives of university mathematics teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: University teaching in mathematics should: (a) answer the requirements of all those who need mathematics for practical purposes; (b) train specialists in the subject; (c) give to all students that intellectual and moral training which any University, worthy of the name, has the duty to impart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These objects are not contradictory but complementary. A training for practical purposes can play the same part as experiments in physics/chemistry. Personal and independent thinking cannot be encouraged without at the same time fostering the spirit of research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem selection and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The study of mathematics consists in the acquisition of useful reflexes and in that of independent habits of thought. The acquisition of useful reflexes should never be separated from the perception of their usefulness. Problem-solving should never be practised for its own sake; particularly tricky problems must be excluded altogether.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The purpose of problems is twofold: either to drill the student in the application of some method of special importance, or to develop his originality by guiding him along some new path. Drill is essentially a school-method and ought to become unnecessary at the final stages of University teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of a proof (criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of a proof means the understanding of its machinery and the ability to reconstruct it. This implies (a) perfect correctness in the definitions; (b) a faculty of connecting a given question with the general ideas underlying it; (c) a perception of the logical nature of any proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The teacher should follow the method related to the most general principles (not merely the quickest or most elegant), point out relations between elements of the hypothesis and the conclusion, and train students to distinguish premises vs conclusion, necessary vs sufficient conditions, and a theorem vs its converse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach to foster independent thinking and research spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal and independent thinking cannot be encouraged without at the same time fostering the spirit of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate opportunities in courses that lead students toward independent inquiry; use problems and exposition that guide students to make connections and to pursue further questions rather than only rote techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make teaching a source of intellectual excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: The teaching of mathematics must be a source of intellectual excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At higher stages, take the student to the brink of the unknown; at earlier stages, make him solve for himself questions of theoretical or practical importance to stimulate curiosity and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value big, simplifying ideas over accumulated details
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is not a science that prospers on details painstakingly collected; the idea often comes forth in full armour from the creator, and the great ideas must be simplifying ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor teaching and research that seek conceptual clarification and simplification of complex technical material rather than celebration of dense technical accumulation; emphasize underlying ideas that unify apparently disparate formulas and concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-emphasize exhaustive technical mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern mathematicians may not know certain historical technical details as well as earlier specialists, but this does not imply those theories must form autonomous sciences; unity of mathematics is more important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curricula and evaluation should not demand encyclopedic mastery of every historical technicality; instead prioritize coherence, unity, and general principles that connect topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and cultivate originality while recognizing its rarity and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical talent usually shows itself at an early age; workers of the second rank play a smaller role — the creator clarifies and often originates major advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that groundbreaking contributions are relatively rare and often early; teaching and mentoring should aim to identify and nurture originality while providing roles for a broader community (e.g., exposition, consolidation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and transmit essential elements of mathematical culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than abandon ourselves to creative work alone, it may be our duty to put the essential elements of our culture in order for the purpose of preserving it, so that descendants may find them intact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of institutional and pedagogical responsibility is the organization, preservation, and clear exposition of core mathematical knowledge and culture for future generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain the honor-driven intellectual attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: If reproached for haughtiness or for pursuing high-level abstract work, the mathematician may answer: 'For the honour of the human spirit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uphold the intrinsic, cultural, and intellectual values of mathematics as legitimate motivations for research and teaching, alongside practical or instrumental justifications.
